messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwesi's Vigil

Kwesi was sixty-eight when the diagnosis came through—stage three pancreatic cancer, delivered by his oncologist with the kind of careful precision that made it sound both technical and final. He had gone to the appointment alone, as he had done most things alone since his wife Ama died five years earlier. The words themselves seemed to arrive from very far away: chemotherapy, survival rates, six to eighteen months. The oncologist's voice was steady, professional, and Kwesi remembered thinking that the man had probably delivered this same sentence a hundred times, that his steadiness was a kindness, though it felt like cruelty. In that moment, sitting in the beige consulting room with its motivational posters about resilience, Kwesi's body had begun its transformation into something he no longer recognized as his own.

The first rounds of chemotherapy came in the winter. Kwesi had worked as a policy analyst for the Department of Health for thirty-two years, and he had always prided himself on his ability to focus—to sit with dense regulatory frameworks and find the logical threads. But by his second month of treatment, he found himself staring at the same paragraph of a policy brief for twenty minutes without absorbing a single sentence. His supervisor had noticed. His colleagues had noticed. The concentration simply would not come. His mind would begin to track something—a data point, a regulatory requirement—and then his attention would scatter, pulled sideways by a sensation in his chest or a tremor in his hands. He had come to believe that the cancer had damaged something essential in his thinking, that he was losing not just his health but his competence, the thing that had made him valuable. He took medical leave in March.

At home, alone in the house he and Ama had bought together in 1989, Kwesi existed in a state of perpetual vigilance. His body had become a stranger that might betray him at any moment. He would be sitting in his study, reading or attempting to read, and suddenly his heart would accelerate wildly, his shoulders would tense to the point of pain, and he would be certain—absolutely certain—that something was wrong, that the cancer had spread, that this was the moment it would take him. The sensations felt like warnings from a body that knew more than he did, a body that was still in the fight for its life even when his conscious mind tried to rest. He found himself unable to relax, even at night. He would lie in bed listening to the house settle around him, every creak registering as a potential threat, his muscles coiled as though danger were about to arrive at any second.

When the memories of the diagnosis came, they arrived with a strange quality of immediacy that terrified him. He would be in the kitchen and suddenly he would be back in that consulting room, the oncologist's face close and serious, the words entering his body like a physical blow. Except it did not feel like memory—it felt like the moment was happening again, that he was receiving the diagnosis for the first time, that the years since had collapsed into nothing. Sometimes the feeling was so overwhelming that he would have to grip the counter, his breath coming short and fast, unable to move until the moment released him. Other times, when he tried to talk about it with his daughter on the phone, he found himself speaking about the diagnosis with a strange flatness, as though he were reporting on someone else's illness, his voice empty of feeling. He would hear himself say the words and feel nothing—no fear, no sadness, only a hollow numbness that somehow frightened him more than the terror did.

What frightened him most was the thought that this—this constant readiness, this body that would no longer obey him, this mind that scattered like startled birds—was permanent. He had come to believe that he would never again feel the quiet contentment he had known before the diagnosis, that his body had become an enemy permanently stationed inside his own skin, and that he could no longer trust it to tell him the truth about what was real and what was merely the echo of fear. His daughter had finally insisted that he see someone, that sitting alone in the house was not healing. It was only when she threatened to move back home, to upend her own life, that Kwesi had agreed to come in. He did so not with hope, but with the exhausted compliance of a man who had already lost so much that he had little left to lose.
